The New York Times did an interactive map of social mobility by county with a slider where you can adjust starting income percentage for a child in a given zip code and see the percentages that end up in each quintile by the time they are 30. Unfortunately there's no ability to see how it averages out across the country but sampling across various counties gives you some idea of what the overall is like.

Everyone focussed on the difficulty of people at the very bottom to make it into the upper quintile. But it's also interesting to see what happens at the top and middle. In most locations a child born in top 1% has an 8-12% chance to end up in the bottom quintile and a similar number end up in second quintile. That means those richest people have at least a few acquaintances from high school who were just as rich but ended up poor or lower middle class. With the advantages they had it's very likely it was not just bad luck but also very bad decisions. So in their personal experience the poor people they know personally ended up poor for entirely predictable reasons due to their poor life choices. Also depending on location only 25-40% of the top 1% stay in the top quintile, That means that more than half of the adults in the top quintile weren't born there but climbed a quintile or two to reach there. 5-10% even climbed from the very bottom. While luck may have played a part in that climb hard work and wise decisions were no doubt necessary as well. So their own experience includes a fair amount of social mobility between the upper and middle classes and even in rarer cases the lower classes.

Even more interesting to me: In most locations the truly middle class at the 50% mark experiences almost perfect social mobility with about 20% of them ending up in each quintile. They go to their high school reunion and the smart, hard working kid is wealthy, the stoner with no motivation is working a minimum wage job or getting by on welfare, the middle of the road kid has a solidly middle-class job much like his father did. Good and bad luck no doubt plays a role but good and bad life choices surely do as well and that is what the middle class sees when they consider social policy.

While technically true, the development side renders this point meaningless.

For starters Android's releases match the hardware capability (as does Apple's releases matches Apple's capabilities) so an Android game designed to run on build 21, or "Lolipop", or Android version 5.0 will run virtually the same on all devices running Build 21 or higher.

The Android SDK even codes in "virtual pixels" so as screen sizes change the game layout does not, the system just scales the pixels accordingly to properly fit the other sized screens. The Dev even has the option on his computer to Emulate any of the Android devices (or create a fictitious one with custom screen sizes) to see how exactly the Virtual Pixels will scale on that device.

In other words, its very easy to properly make a game compatible across various Android devices, generally. The SDK is designed to make that one of the more easy aspects of the process.

Personally I find coding for Android a nightmare, not because of all the different builds but because of the architecture Android uses. I makes sense, but damn its not intuitive to me at all. I'd much rather work in C# files or Python files, than page after page after page of XML. One simple UI field takes making edits to 4 or 5 different files. All that can be automated but then you get overhead and such.

I have no clue what coding for Apple is like. I imagine they have the exact same issues as Android, if not worse, because Android has spent so much time making its multiple platforms and builds cross compatible and simple to code for, where as Apple is notorious for mandating things and rigid structural adherence for each device.

Advice on textbooks to add to my library

It's not strictly a text book and not really related to your interests but I always recommend Richard Feynman's Quantum Electrodynamics to anyone interested in science or engineering. As an engineer, it is one of my favorite books.

EDIT: Also, while I'm being completely of no help to you, I'd also recommend Thomas S. Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolution. It's an insightful and relevant look into how and why scientific theories progress the way that they do.
A vendor of mine gave me a book from Emerson called "Engineer's Guide to Industrial Temperature Measurement". It's a good'n.
Get some catalogs too, specifically MSC, McMaster, Grainger, and Omega. Great reference material and bathroom books.

To focused. Get copies of Gas Turbine Theory Cohen & Saravanamuttoo and Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer by Bergman. These books should cover everything except HVAC cant help you with that.
